subject: anatomy
title: Pectoral Girdle Muscles and Breast Lymphatic Drainage

steps.tx: The anterior chest wall is dominated by the **pectoralis major**, a massive fan-shaped muscle possessing clavicular and sternocostal heads. The clavicular head arises from the medial half of the clavicle, while the sternocostal head arises from the sternum and upper six costal cartilages. Both heads converge into a U-shaped bilaminar tendon inserting into the lateral lip of the bicipital groove.
steps.say: The anterior chest wall is dominated by the pectoralis major, featuring clavicular and sternocostal heads. The clavicular head arises from the medial clavicle and the sternocostal head from the sternum and ribs. Both insert into the lateral lip of the bicipital groove.

vis.caption: Pectoral musculature and anatomical relationships of the female breast. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Innervated by both lateral and medial pectoral nerves, the pectoralis major acts as a powerful adductor and medial rotator of the arm, while its clavicular fibres assist in arm flexion. Deep to pectoralis major lies **pectoralis minor**, arising from ribs three, four, and five and inserting into the coracoid process, innervated by the medial pectoral nerve.
steps.say: Supplied by lateral and medial pectoral nerves, pectoralis major adducts and medially rotates the humerus. Deep to it lies pectoralis minor, arising from ribs three to five and inserting into the coracoid process, supplied by the medial pectoral nerve.

points: Dual nerve supply: Lateral and medial pectoral
Inserts into lateral lip of bicipital groove

right.title: Pectoralis Minor
points: Innervated purely by medial pectoral nerve
Inserts onto the coracoid process of scapula

steps.tx: Suspended between the clavicle and the upper border of pectoralis minor is the **clavipectoral fascia**, which splits to enclose subclavius above and pectoralis minor below. This fascia is pierced by four distinct neurovascular structures: the cephalic vein, the thoracoacromial artery, the lateral pectoral nerve, and lymphatic trunks draining the infraclavicular nodes.
steps.say: Stretching from the clavicle to pectoralis minor is the clavipectoral fascia. This tough sheet is pierced by four structures: the cephalic vein, thoracoacromial artery, lateral pectoral nerve, and lymphatic trunks draining toward the axilla.

steps.tx: The female breast extends vertically from the second to the sixth rib, and transversely from the lateral sternal border to the midaxillary line. Its superolateral extension pierces the deep axillary fascia through the foramen of Langer into the axilla as the **axillary tail of Spence**. It rests upon deep pectoral fascia separated by the retromammary space.
steps.say: The female breast spans from the second to sixth rib and from the sternal edge to the midaxillary line. Its superolateral extension penetrates the axillary fascia as the axillary tail of Spence. It glides over deep pectoral fascia across the retromammary space.

steps.tx: The glandular parenchyma is suspended from the overlying dermis by strong fibrous bands designated **suspensory ligaments of Cooper**. Malignant infiltration of these ligaments by breast carcinoma causes pathological shortening that pulls the overlying skin inward, creating the characteristic clinical sign of localized skin dimpling or tethering.
steps.say: Glandular lobules are suspended from skin by fibrous suspensory ligaments of Cooper. Infiltration of these bands by breast cancer causes retraction, pulling the skin inward to produce localized dimpling.

left.title: Cooper Ligament Infiltration
points: Tumour cells invade fibrous suspensory bands

right.title: Dermal Lymphatic Obstruction
points: Hair follicles remain tethered to deep dermis

steps.tx: When malignant tumor emboli block the subdermal lymphatic plexus, localized cutaneous edema develops while hair follicles remain tethered by sweat gland ducts, producing the pitted orange-peel texture known as **peau d orange**. Cancer invasion into the main lactiferous ducts behind the areola triggers fibrous ductal contraction, presenting clinically as nipple retraction.
steps.say: When tumour emboli plug subdermal lymphatics, skin lymphedema develops around tethered hair follicles, yielding the pitted peau d orange texture. Malignant invasion of lactiferous ducts pulls the nipple inward, causing nipple retraction.

steps.tx: Lymphatic drainage of the breast is paramount in staging carcinoma: seventy-five percent drains laterally into the **axillary lymph nodes**, twenty percent drains medially into internal mammary nodes along the internal thoracic artery, and five percent drains into posterior intercostal nodes. Surgical staging categorizes axillary nodes into three levels relative to the pectoralis minor muscle.
steps.say: Seventy-five percent of breast lymph drains into axillary nodes, twenty percent passes to internal mammary nodes, and five percent enters posterior intercostal channels. Axillary lymph nodes are classified into three surgical levels relative to pectoralis minor.

rows: Lateral to lateral border of pectoralis minor
Central axillary group, interpectoral Rotter nodes
Cleared in standard level I and II dissection
Medial to medial border of pectoralis minor
Parasternal spaces along internal thoracic artery

steps.tx: Level I nodes lie lateral to pectoralis minor; Level II nodes lie directly posterior to pectoralis minor; Level III nodes lie medial to pectoralis minor beneath the clavicle. To minimize morbidity from extensive axillary lymphadenectomy, clinicians perform a **sentinel node biopsy** by injecting radiotracer or blue dye into the periareolar plexus, mapping the first draining station node.
steps.say: Level one nodes lie lateral to pectoralis minor, level two sit deep to it, and level three sit medial. To avoid unnecessary axillary clearance, surgeons perform sentinel node biopsy using blue dye or radiotracer to identify the first draining node.
